# Overview

## Package Description

The `@ps-refarch/district-settings` package provides a webhook to capture district onboarding (`addDistrict`) and offboarding (`removeDistrict`) events from District Settings (aka Unified Customer Configuration). Once captured, it creates or updates a district-specific entry in the `tenants` table, a DynamoDB table in the same account and region. It also publishes an appropriate event onto an EventBridge event bus, where the application can add targets to handle when a district onboarding/offboarding action occurs.

**Note**: Only the onboarding action is currently fully implemented, because District Settings does not as of this writing send a webhook when products are removed from the district.

## Note on "environment" and "namespace" names

Many of the configuration items of this package's constructs talk about two similar-sounding and related names:
* The "environment name" (sometimes abbreviated as `envName`), which refers to a specific deployment of the Reference Architecture application in AWS.
* The "namespace", which refers to a level of deployments of the Reference Architecture application.

For most Reference Architecture applications, there are four "namespaces":
* `dev`, which is used by the development team for development purposes
* `int`, which is used primarily by the QA team, and is the primary place where QA testing is done
* `stgus`, which is also used primarily by the QA team, it is where all the applications can be seen together in one place, and we can test for (probably unwanted) interactions between them.
* `produs`, which is the production system seen by customers.

For anything past `dev`, the "namespace" is always the same as the "environment name". In `dev`, there are two options:
* The application's main branch is always deployed directly into the fixed `dev` environment. Like the other namespace/environments, there is only one `dev`.
* Developers can do personal or "feature branch" deployments to other environment names, all of which come under the `dev` namespace. Because we are following GitOps processes, the feature branch environment names are by convention the same as the git branch name, and always are prefixed by `dev/` since they are in the `dev` namespace. So a branch name might be `dev/ESP-1234`, which deploys into the `dev/ESP-1234` environment name (which is in the `dev` namespace).

# Installation

To install, add to your project:
```
npm install @ps-refarch/district-settings
```

# Usage

## Dependencies

The package has the following internal `@ps-refarch` dependencies:

* [`@ps-refarch/cdk-utils`](../../cdk-utils/index.html)
* `@ps-refarch/env-vars`
* [`@ps-refarch/lambda-utils`](../../lambda-utils/docs/index.html)
* [`@ps-refarch/tenants`](../../tenants/docs/index.html)

## Examples

Here's an example of usage. Typically this package is used together with [`@ps-refarch/tenants`](../../tenants/docs), which creates a table for all the districts/tenants/unified customers (names vary, obviously...) for the current application/product.

```typescript
    // Access (or create) the tenants table
    const tenants = new TenantsV2(this, 'Tenants Table', {
      env: appStackProps.env,
      environmentName: envName,
      namespace,
      lambdaVars: flags.lambdaVars,
    });

    // Create the district settings webhook. Note that for feature branches,
    // there won't be any verification of the JWT.
    const districtSettings = new DistrictSettings(this, 'District Settings', {
      environmentName: envName,
      namespace,
      isProduction,
      lambdaVars: flags.lambdaVars,
      tenantsTable: tenants.tenantsTable,
      api
      testOnlyNoVerifyJWT: isFeatureBranch
    });
```

## Configuration

The `DistrictSettings` construct has the following common properties. For full description, see [`District Settings`](./classes/cdk_lib.DistrictSettings.html).

|Key|Type|Meaning|
|---|----|-------|
|`environmentName`|string|The "environment name" (see note above).|
|`namespace`|string|The "namespace" (see note above).|
|`lambdaVars`|`Record<string,string>`|Common environment variables passed to Lambdas.|
|`tenantsTable`|DynamoDB `ITable`|The DynamoDB table to track tenants. Normally, this is created by the `TenantsV2` construct of the [`@ps-refarch/tenants`](../../tenants/doc) package.|
|`issuer`|string|District Settings Issuer, used for validating JWTs. Normally something like `https://int.services.powerschoolcorp.com/`|
|`testOnlyNoVerifyJWT`|boolean (default `false`)|If `true`, do not verify the JWT from District Settings. This is clearly extremely unsafe for "real" usage, and should generally only be used in Feature Branches, where manual testing with a tool like Postman is desired.|

## Credentials and Secrets Manager

You need to set a secret credential value to contact District Settings API. FORMERLY, this was stored in the Secret `districtSettings/<namespace>` where `namespace` is typically dev/int/stgus/produs. However, this was confusing, because you can actually have two different kinds of District Settings credentials:

* The old style, which is stored in AWS Cognito. You get an access token using an endpoint like `https://auth.services.powerschool.com/oauth2/token` or `	
https://auth.int.services.powerschoolcorp.com/oauth2/token`
* The new style, which is stored in Auth0. You get an access token using an endpoint like `https://auth.powerschool.com/oauth/token` or `https://int.auth.powerschoolcorp.com/oauth/token`

Until version 0.14, the District Settings construct (and webhook, and exported `callDistrictSettings` function) supported both types of credentials. This made the code messy, led to additional M2M tokens being created, and was confusing and error-prone. So with v0.14, ONLY the new style (auth0) is supported. The District Settings team is moving everybody off cognito anyway, so it will just be a matter of time; better to make the change now, when very few teams are using District Settings construct.

Now, we just use auth0 credentials like anything else using @ps-refarch/uu-utils. By default it uses the `common` logical client, but you can change that if necessary using the `logicalClientId` construct property.

## Bring your own API Gateway

Normally, the construct creates its own API Gateway. This can be handy, but sometimes you'll want to bring your own. This can be done by passing the `api` property to the construct. However, there's a trap here for the unwary. If the API gateway you pass comes from the `Api` or `BFFApi` constructs in the `@ps-refarch/bff-api` package,
and you are using IAM in any of your other endpoints, you will also need to pass in the `resourcePolicy` property so the policy can be modified to allow District Settings to access our endpoints. Note that this is technically only necessary if you use IAM authentication, but it won't hurt to pass in the `_policy` property regardless: if
IAM authentication is not being used in the API Gateway, `_policy` will be undefined, and it will be ignored.

Here's a typical usage:

```
  // Create our RestAPI
  const bffApi = new BFFApi(this, 'My API', { ... });

  // Create District Settings interface attached to our existing API
  const districtSettings = new DistrictSettings(this, 'District Settings', {
    environmentName: envName,
    namespace,
    isProduction,
    lambdaVars: flags.lambdaVars,
    tenantsTable: tenants.tenantsTable,
    testOnlyNoVerifyJWT: envName.startsWith('dev'),
    sharedServiceEnv,
    fillFromDistrictSettings: true,
    api: bffApi.api,                      // Bring your own API
    // eslint-disable-next-line no-underscore-dangle
    resourcePolicy: bffApi._policy        // Technically only necessary if you use IAM authentication
  });
```
